about: Skills tool: Hardy-Weinberg calculations. Solver and generator: ApBioProblems, kind hw (mode counts or recessive). Built now, published with Unit 7: every item is tagged stats-hardy-weinberg, whose map entry sits after the Unit 7 topic hardy-weinberg, so the generator serves it only once Unit 7 is published.
intro: Drag the allele frequency and watch a bed of 100 snapdragons change, then find allele frequencies from genotype counts or from the share of individuals showing a recessive trait, and predict genotype frequencies for a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
howItWorksTitle: The equations, their assumptions, and how answers are checked
howItWorks:
p + q = 1

p² + 2pq + q² = 1

  • p and q are the frequencies of the two alleles of one gene; p², 2pq and q² are the expected frequencies of the two homozygous genotypes and the heterozygote.
  • From genotype counts, count alleles: every individual carries two. From a recessive phenotype, q² is the share of individuals showing it, because only homozygous recessive individuals do.
  • The genotype frequencies are expected only if the population is in equilibrium: very large, mating at random, with no mutation, no migration and no natural selection.
  • Frequencies count when within one unit of the last decimal place asked for (0.01 for p, q and 2pq; 0.001 for q²) or 1%; numbers of individuals within 2%.

explore.about: Explore (tools v2, docs/tools-v2-hardy-weinberg-brief.md): a bed of side x side snapdragons. Each plant gets the allele of its column's pollen grain and of its row's egg; p is the share of R among both. Flower color shows incomplete dominance, so every genotype can be seen.
explore.purpose: With random mating, allele frequencies set the genotypes
explore.note: The bed is a model: 100 snapdragons sorted so they can be counted. In a real population the same shares are scattered at random. R and W stand for the snapdragon alleles C<sup>R</sup> and C<sup>W</sup>; flower color shows incomplete dominance, so RR plants are red, RW plants are pink and WW plants are white.

pea.about: Test yourself, the targets about a hidden recessive (sp: "pea"): a bed of pea plants, flower colour with complete dominance (OpenStax 12.2: purple dominant over white). AA and Aa plants are both purple; only aa plants show white.
pea.name: pea plants

targets.ask: Set the alleles so that 16% of the pea plants show the recessive trait (white flowers).
targets.hint: Only aa plants show white. Their share is q².
targets.why: Only the white plants can be read straight off the bed: they are aa, so q² = 0.16. Then q = √0.16 = 0.4 and p = 1 − q = 0.6. Every purple plant is AA or Aa and looks the same: purple is p² + 2pq = 0.36 + 0.48 = 0.84, and 48% of the bed are carriers (Aa), purple but carrying a.

targets.ask: Set the alleles for the most pink plants a bed can have.
targets.hint: Pink plants are RW. Their share is 2pq.
targets.why: 2pq is largest when p = q = 0.5. Then half the plants are heterozygous: the most any population can have at equilibrium.

targets.ask: Make the recessive trait rare: just 1% of the pea plants with white flowers. Then count the carriers.
targets.hint: Only aa plants show white. Their share is q².
targets.why: q² = 0.01, so q = 0.1 and p = 0.9. Only 1% of the plants show white, but 2pq = 18% are carriers (Aa): purple, and carrying a. Most copies of a rare recessive allele hide in carriers, where nobody can see them.

targets.ask: Set the alleles so that 49% of the plants bloom red.
targets.hint: Red plants are RR. Their share is p².
targets.why: Red plants are RR, so p² = 0.49 and p = √0.49 = 0.7. Then q = 0.3.

targets.ask: Set the alleles so that 32% of the plants bloom pink.
targets.hint: Pink plants are RW. Their share is 2pq, and p + q = 1.
targets.why: 2pq = 0.32 when p and q are 0.8 and 0.2, either way round: 2 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.32. Two different gene pools give the same share of heterozygotes.
